summary:
Guinea criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. Article 274 of the 2016 Penal Code punishes it with six months to three years' imprisonment, a fine of GNF 500,000 to 1,000,000, or both; the 1998 code's Article 325, still cited under the indecency provisions in the US State Department's 2023 Human Rights Report, covered the same conduct and carried a lower minimum fine. Where violence or attempted violence accompanies the act, sentences rise to five to ten years, and conduct involving a person under 21 triggers the maximum penalty.

Enforcement does not depend on proof of conduct. Police arrest people on the basis of clothing and appearance, the statute operates as a basis for extortion, and release is commonly secured by payment to police. Afrique Arc-en-Ciel Conakry reported gay men jailed and fined for release in 2016 and 2017, and in 2023 the Office for the Protection of Women, Children, and Morals added a unit to investigate same-sex conduct. A 2024 Universal Periodic Review stakeholder submission records LGBTQ people held for up to five days despite the 48-hour legal limit, most released only after paying bribes or fines.

Transgender women face a specific and documented pattern: arrest and imprisonment on the stated pretext of protecting them from community violence, followed by detention in male prisons where they often experience sexual violence. LGBTQ people in custody are frequently abused, and security forces have arrested, harassed and used violence against LGBTQ people accused of disrupting social order.

The Advocates for Human Rights and Khaleem Ali's joint stakeholder report to the Universal Periodic Review of October 2024 describes arbitrary arrest, harassment and extortion by police within a hostile and sometimes deadly environment, with threats of physical violence and discrimination on grounds of orientation, gender identity and expression. Widespread stigmatisation deters reporting of violence.

There is no legal gender recognition and no recognition of same-sex unions. Discrimination in healthcare, housing, education and employment is documented, and no law protects LGBTQ people from discrimination in health services. Families arrange forced heterosexual marriages, and religious, cultural and familial pressure is applied to attempt to convert LGBTQ people, falling most heavily on younger people.

Law L/2024/001/CNT/SGG of January 12, 2024 on HIV Prevention, Care, and Protection defines members of sexual minorities to include gays, lesbians, bisexuals, intersex and transgender people whether or not they self-identify, and Ordinance No. 056/2009/PRG/SGG on HIV/AIDS lists sexual minorities as a vulnerable and marginalised group. The definitions are protective in intent but also mark transgender people for administrative identification regardless of self-identification.

Section 9.9.30(b) of the Guinea Aeronautical Regulations (2022), issued by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, bars competent government agencies from using Passenger Name Record data that reveals an individual's sex life or sexual orientation alongside racial, ethnic, political, religious, trade-union or health data. The text gives no further detail on entry screening, visa rules or border checks for trans or LGBTQ travellers.

Public hostility is measurable and official hostility has been stated openly. A survey spanning 2021 to 2023 found that 87 percent of Guineans would dislike or strongly dislike having a gay neighbour, and the US State Department's 2011 report described homosexuality as socially, religiously and culturally taboo. In 2010 Prime Minister Lansana Kouyate stated that consensual same-sex activity was wrong and should be illegal and that sexual orientation should not be a human right. The 2023 report found that most LGBTQ Guineans do not disclose publicly, that there is no substantial political presence of openly LGBTQ people, and that LGBTQ people are cast as part of a Western imperialist agenda attributed to the United States and France; some LGBTQ Guineans have been internally displaced to escape areas whose religious and cultural norms endanger them.
tangentialFactors:
The two US State Department reports a decade apart show a shift in the visibility of organised advocacy rather than in the law. The 2011 report recorded societal discrimination and no LGBTQ organisations in the country; the 2023 report found that LGBTQ groups do exist but cannot obtain legal recognition despite no law barring it, and that openly LGBTQ people have no substantial political presence.

The 2011 report also documented security-force torture, prison abuse and female genital mutilation, which bear on conditions of detention for anyone remanded in custody rather than on trans status alone.

The 2016 Penal Code raised the minimum fine above the 1998 text while keeping the same order of imprisonment, so the direction of legislative change has been toward heavier penalty rather than decriminalisation. No source in the inventory records a challenge to Article 274 or a decriminalisation bill before the courts or the legislature.
localsOnly:
Adoption under Guinean law is open to a couple married at least five years or to an unmarried person aged at least 30 with a 15-year age gap, and the law does not specifically bar LGBTQ people from adopting; no source records how the provision is applied in practice.

Guinean law provides no legal gender recognition, so transgender residents have no route to amend the sex marker on civil documents, and no source records an administrative procedure or court remedy for doing so.

The HIV statutes of 2009 and January 2024 name sexual minorities, including transgender people, as a defined category for prevention and care purposes. Ordinance No. 056/2009/PRG/SGG lists them as a vulnerable and marginalised group, while no law protects them from discrimination when seeking health services.

Discrimination in housing, education and employment is documented, and internal displacement is reported for LGBTQ Guineans who have left areas whose religious and cultural norms endanger them. Conversion pressure from family, religious and cultural sources is directed most intensely at younger people, alongside arranged heterosexual marriages.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory states whether Guinea's immigration or visa authorities impose any trans-specific entry requirement, whether a passport sex-marker change is accepted for entry, or how gender markers are handled at border control. The Aeronautical Regulations' Passenger Name Record provision addresses data use by government agencies and says nothing about screening practice, so its effect on a trans traveller at arrival is unresolved.

Whether the Passenger Name Record restriction is enforced in practice, and which agencies hold such data, is not sourced here.

No information is available in the inventory on access to gender-affirming healthcare, on the availability of hormone therapy, or on whether the healthcare discrimination documented extends to trans-specific treatment.

Reports of transgender women held in male prisons and subjected to sexual violence are drawn from stakeholder submissions and secondary compilation; the number of cases, the facilities concerned and any prosecutions or disciplinary outcomes are not sourced.

Post-2024 judicial or legislative developments on Article 274, and any change to the 2023 unit within the Office for the Protection of Women, Children, and Morals, are unresolved in this inventory.
